chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, and Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, all from Ibn Abi Umayr, from Hammad, from Al-Halaby, who said:

Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) was asked about a man who advanced his dirhams for five sealed containers of wheat or barley for a specified term, and the one who owed the wheat and barley was unable to repay all of what was due to him when it became due. So he asked the owner of the right (the buyer) to take half of the foodstuff, or a third, or less than that, or more, and take back the capital of what remained of the foodstuff in dirhams. He (peace be upon him) said: 'There is no problem.'

And regarding saffron, a man advances his dirhams for twenty mithqals, or less than that or more. He (peace be upon him) said: 'There is no problem if the one who owes the saffron is unable to give him all of his goods, that he take half of his right, or a third, or two-thirds, and take back the capital of what remains from his right.'
ai.seo_question: What are the Islamic legal rulings for advance payment in trade when the seller cannot deliver the full amount of goods?
ai.summary: Imam al-Sadiq (AS) validates the permissibility of 'salb' (advance payment) for specific commodities like wheat, barley, and saffran, addressing the practical issue of default where the debtor cannot fulfill the entire obligation. The ruling allows the creditor to accept a partial delivery of goods while recovering the cash value of the remainder, reflecting the Shia juristic principle of flexibility in debt settlement to prevent hardship. This precedent underscores the importance of equitable commercial practices in Islamic finance, ensuring that creditors are not left with unfulfilled promises while debtors are not burdened beyond their capacity.
